title: Nitrate pollution in rivers linked to dry climates, not just human activity
summary: Nitrate, a chemical compound of oxygen and nitrogen often used in farm fertilizers, can rise to toxic levels in surrounding water under very dry conditions. This relationship has traditionally been attributed to agricultural runoff or human waste in the environment, but new research led by scientists at Penn State shows that a hot and dry climate elevates concentrations of nitrate in rivers and streams, even in areas without urban or agricultural development.

Credit: Li Li Nitrate, a chemical compound of oxygen and nitrogen often used in farm fertilizers, can rise to toxic levels in surrounding water under very dry conditions. This relationship has traditionally been attributed to agricultural runoff or human waste in the environment, but new research led by scientists at Penn State shows that a hot and dry climate elevates concentrations of nitrate in rivers and streams, even in areas without urban or agricultural development. Using artificial intelligence (AI) algorithms to overlay data patterns recorded from more than 7,000 river sites around the world, the team built a machine learning model that can reliably map nitrate concentrations across regions with scarce data. Their research, which the team said is the first of its kind at a global scale, suggests that nitrate pollution is not driven by human activity alone—climate conditions also play a critical role. They published their findings on Nov. 12 in Science . "Right now, roughly a half-billion people are living in proximity to rivers where nitrate concentrations exceed levels that can potentially lead to negative health effects," said Li Li, the Barry and Shirley Isett professor of environmental engineering and corresponding author on the paper. "This finding implies that nitrate pollution is beyond a local management issue: It's a broader problem directly related to climate, which is becoming increasingly hotter and drier." The team's global map of predicted riverine nitrate concentrations reveals unexpectedly elevated concentrations in arid, remote regions beyond expected hot spots with high human inputs. Credit: Li Li/Kayalvizhi Sadayappan Health risks below the regulatory limit Nitrate is one of the most prevalent forms of inorganic pollution found in rivers, streams, lakes and groundwater worldwide , with about 18% of the U.S. population exposed to drinking water with elevated nitrate levels between 2021 and 2023. In addition to harming ecosystems, high levels of nitrate in drinking water can lead to a host of health conditions, most notably methemoglobinemia—commonly known as blue baby syndrome—a potentially fatal condition in which an infant's blood cannot effectively carry oxygen. "Generally, we think nitrate hot spots derive from human input like fertilizer used in agriculture or wastewater from cities," said Li, who holds an additional affiliation with Penn State's Institute of Energy and the Environment. "There's not a lot of very large-scale water quality work, so people don't traditionally think about climate in terms of affecting nitrate levels. However, our new model is telling us that although human input plays a major role, long-term climate such as average annual temperature and average annual rainfall of an area contributes to environmental nitrate levels, as well." Nitrate occurs naturally in low concentrations, but heavily farmed areas like the Corn Belt, a portion of the U.S. Midwest spanning from Nebraska to Ohio, exhibit some of the highest nitrate concentrations on Earth, said Kayalvizhi Sadayappan, a postdoctoral scholar in civil and environmental engineering and first author on the paper. Current regulatory standards exist to protect against adverse health impacts, but Sadayappan said that nitrate can still carry risks at lower levels. "For nitrate, we have a regulatory standard set at 10 milligrams of nitrate per liter of water, primarily to prevent acute diseases like blue baby syndrome," Sadayappan said. "This has been the standard since the 1970s, but scientists are now observing that slower, chronic conditions like cancers or issues related to reproduction can be linked to exposure at much lower levels, like 2.5 milligrams of nitrate per liter of water." Subscribe Mapping nitrate where monitoring is scarce The model works by aggregating millions of individual nitrate readings taken from more than 7,000 river segments and using patterns observed in these data to train it to make predictions. Li explained that a portion of these readings are withheld from the training data set so that predictions can be compared to real data the model has not processed, allowing the team to evaluate the model's accuracy.
